svg.text: Three things a trap entry may not assume
Every one of them held for a shallow call graph and a warm TLB, which is why a freestanding test passed for eleven sections while a dynamically linked program could not start.
A. NOTHING MAY BE LIVE IN A GLOBAL ACROSS THE ENTRY `save`
A trap arriving with CANSAVE at zero has no free window, so the save in the trap entry spills before it completes. The spill handler needs
scratch registers, and the only ones it has are globals — and a trap taken at trap level one does not get a fresh bank. The hardware selects
the alternate globals on entry; they are already selected; the handler and the entry hold the same physical registers.
So retry re-runs the save with whatever the spill handler left behind.
WAS — the address computed before the save
ldx [%g7 + KERNEL_STACK], %g2
sub %g2, FRAME, %g2
save %g2, %g0, %sp
andcc %g1, TSTATE_PRIV, %g0
When that save spills, SPILL_USER_WINDOW runs and ends with
ldx [%g7 + OTHER_SPILL_COUNT], %g2 ; inc ; stx
so %g2 is the number of spills this thread has taken.
%sp became 46. %g1 held TSTATE and went the same way.
IS — everything derived after it
save %sp, -FRAME, %sp
rdpr %tstate, %l0
andcc %l0, TSTATE_PRIV, %g0
ldx [%g7 + KERNEL_STACK], %l1
sub %l1, FRAME, %sp
The operands are %sp and a constant — right for a trap out of
the kernel, harmless for one out of userspace, because `save`
only does arithmetic and %sp is overwritten before any store.
Locals are window registers: a spill cannot reach them.
B. CLEANWIN ONLY EVER GROWS, SO CLEANING ONCE IS NOT CLEANING
The clean_window handler zeroes a window and increments CLEANWIN — tens of thousands of times a boot, as the kernel works through its
own call graph. Nothing lowers it again; flushw does not, because spilling a window says nothing about whether it was scrubbed.
Lowered once, at thread start
The first window a thread enters is clean. The kernel takes its
next trap long before userspace takes its second, so every
window after the first carries the kernel's %l0–%l7.
Lowered on every return to userspace
CLEANWIN := CANRESTORE − 1, because the `restore` below has
not happened yet and the equality that forces the next `save`
to trap has to hold afterwards. Guarded: zero already forces it.
What userspace received was not arbitrary: the kernel's most recent use of any window is the trap entry itself, so a dirty window handed
to a program held %l0 = TSTATE, %l1 = the trapped %tpc, %l2 = %tnpc, %l3 = the trap number. Programs write only the locals they have a
use for, so the rest were still there when the window spilled — to the user's own stack.
C. THE FAULTING ADDRESS SURVIVES ONLY UNTIL THE NEXT D-MMU MISS
The D-MMU rewrites Tag Access on every miss, including the fast ones the kernel resolves in the trap table without any of this running.
← seven stores to a kernel stack a freshly scheduled thread may not have in the TLB
ldxa [TAG_ACCESS] ASI_DMMU
← reads whichever of those missed, not the address userspace faulted on
The comment above that read said “before anything else can overwrite them”, and it was written in good faith: a list of registers being
saved does not read as memory traffic. It now happens in the first instruction of sparc_fault_entry, recorded in the trap data block —
which has its own locked D-TLB entry precisely so that a store from a handler cannot itself miss.
